newsitem.title: UK: Sleaze dogs Major on UK election trail.
newsitem.headline: Sleaze dogs Major on UK election trail.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party, seeking more political capital from new sleaze allegations against a ruling Conservative member of parliament, tried to draw in Prime Minister John Major on Thursday with taunts of weak leadership.

But, as pressure built on MP Piers Merchant to step down ahead of a general election on May 1 after press reports that he had an affair with a 17-year-old nightclub hostess, ministers trained their fire on the media, accusing reporters of acting like a lynch mob.

The latest blow for Major's Conservatives came a day after a former junior minister, Tim Smith, quit as a candidate over his failure to declare accepting cash for asking questions in parliament, overshadowing Conservative attacks on Labour's links with the trade union movement.
Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine described the latest scandal as an embarrassment for his party.
"These revelations, accusations, headlines are a damaging diversion in an election campaign," Heseltine told BBC radio.

As a new poll showed Labour maintaining a lead of more than 20 percentage points over the Conservatives, Labour's economics and finance spokesman, Gordon Brown, challenged Major to answer questions about the suitability of other candidates already under investigation by a parliamentary ethics watchdog body.
"This has now moved beyond a question of the behaviour of Tory MPs to a question of leadership," Brown told a news conference.
"(It is a question of) his failure to control his party, his failure to take action against the MPs who asked questions for money, his broken promises."
The latest scandal broke in The Sun newspaper, which last week declared its support for the main opposition Labour Party.
The nation's top-selling tabloid printed a series of photographs showing the married Merchant kissing blonde teenager Anna Cox.
The MP denied the story, telling The Sun: "Anna is a dear friend of mine and has been helping my campaign. But there is no question of us having an affair. I have never made love to her."
But the Sun's revelations gave new life to Labour charges that the government was mired in sleaze.
A committee of MPs has been looking into allegationss that money was clandestinely paid to Smith and to nine other Conservative MPs to ask questions in parliament.
But Major's decision to close parliament last Friday meant the report could not be published before the election, prompting Labour to accuse the prime minister of a cover-up.
Defence Secretary Michael Portillo sought to blame the media.

"What I think would be really damaging to this country would be trial by media, the lynch mob, decisions and judgments made on incomplete evidence, people condemned who have not had the chance to speak up in their defence," Portillo said.
But pressure mounted on Thursday for Merchant to quit.
"I haven't the slightest doubt that Piers Merchant, his family and his association will want to consider very carefully the consequences of what has happened for the party at large," Heseltine said.

And, as Conservative anger mounted that sleaze looked like dominating the campaign over the Easter weekend, Major used similar language, saying Merchant "will want to explain the stories in this morning's press to his constituents and others".
